Project Description – FieldShift

FieldShift is a data-driven agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers adapt to changing weather and climate conditions using NASA Earth observation data. The platform brings together information from NASA datasets, including SMAP (soil moisture), IMERG (precipitation), MODIS (vegetation and land surface observations), and NASA POWER (weather and solar-related data), alongside weather forecasts. It processes these datasets to provide useful agricultural insights and recommendations for important farming activities such as deciding when to sow, monitoring crop maturity, planning harvesting and threshing, and making crop rotation decisions.

The main benefit of FieldShift is that it transforms complex satellite and weather data into practical information that can support better farming decisions. Instead of relying only on traditional knowledge or general weather expectations, farmers can use environmental indicators to understand changing field conditions, anticipate potential risks, and make more informed decisions. The intended impact is to improve agricultural resilience, reduce losses caused by unpredictable weather, support more efficient use of agricultural resources, and contribute to food security, particularly in communities vulnerable to climate variability.

The project was developed using modern web technologies. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite to provide an interactive user interface, while the backend uses Node.js, Express, and TypeScript to handle application logic, data processing, and API integrations. PostgreSQL is used for database management. The project integrates NASA data services and weather information through APIs, including SMAP, IMERG, MODIS, and NASA POWER.

What makes FieldShift creative is its focus on connecting multiple NASA Earth observation datasets to specific agricultural decisions rather than simply displaying satellite data or weather information. It aims to turn environmental observations into actionable guidance across different stages of farming, from sowing to harvesting and beyond. This makes the platform more than a weather dashboard: it is designed as a practical decision-support tool for agriculture.

During development, our team considered several important factors, including the reliability and relevance of NASA datasets, the relationship between environmental conditions and farming activities, changing weather patterns, the usefulness of recommendations, and the need to present technical information in an understandable way. We also considered the accessibility of open data and APIs, the limitations of satellite observations, and the importance of building a platform that can be extended to support different crops and agricultural regions.
